$f(x) = 3x^2 - x$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{3(x+h)^2 - (x+h) - (3x^2 - x)}{h}\\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{3(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) - x - h - 3x^2 + x}{h}\\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{6xh + 3h^2 - h}{h}\\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{h(6x + 3h - 1)}{h}\\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}(6x + 3h - 1)\\ f'(x) &= 6x - 1 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.question: 17(d)
solutions.latex:
Let $m = \log_e x$.

$$m - \dfrac{3}{m} = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; m^2 - 3 = 2m \;\Rightarrow\; m^2 - 2m - 3 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (m-3)(m+1) = 0$$

$m = 3$: $\log_e x = 3$, $x = e^3$.

$m = -1$: $\log_e x = -1$, $x = e^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{e}$.

$$300 = \dfrac{1}{2}n(n+9) \;\Rightarrow\; 600 = n^2 + 9n \;\Rightarrow\; 0 = n^2 + 9n - 600$$

$$n = \dfrac{-9 \pm\sqrt{9^2 - 4(1)(-600)}}{2} = 20.4 \text{ or } -29.4$$

So 20 rows can be created.

Using $1 + \cot^2 x = \operatorname{cosec}^2 x$:

$$\begin{aligned} 5(\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - 1) - 2\operatorname{cosec}x + 2 &= 5\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - 5 - 2\operatorname{cosec}x + 2\\ &= 5\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - 2\operatorname{cosec}x - 3 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 5\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - 2\operatorname{cosec}x - 3 &= 0\\ 5\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - 5\operatorname{cosec}x + 3\operatorname{cosec}x - 3 &= 0\\ 5\operatorname{cosec}x(\operatorname{cosec}x - 1) + 3(\operatorname{cosec}x - 1) &= 0\\ (\operatorname{cosec}x - 1)(5\operatorname{cosec}x + 3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$\operatorname{cosec}x = 1$ gives $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$; $\operatorname{cosec}x = -\dfrac{3}{5}$ has no solution.

So $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is the only solution.

$r = -\tan^2 x$. For a limiting sum: $-1 < -\tan^2 x < 1$, so $-1 < \tan^2 x < 1$, so $-1 < \tan x < 1$.

$$S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r} = \dfrac{1}{1 - (-\tan^2 x)} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \tan^2 x} = \dfrac{1}{\sec^2 x} = \cos^2 x$$

$\dfrac{1}{4} = \cos^2 x$, so $\cos x = \pm\dfrac{1}{2}$, giving $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

The solution must lie in $0 \le x < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $\dfrac{3\pi}{4} < x \le \pi$, $\pi \le x < \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ or $\dfrac{7\pi}{4} < x \le 2\pi$.

Since all the solutions above do not lie within the permitted values of $r$, there is no solution.

$y' = x^3 - 3x^2 = x^2(x-3) = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = 3$. When $x = 0$, $y = 0$; when $x = 3$, $y = -\dfrac{27}{4}$.

Stationary points: $(0,0)$ and $\left(3, -\dfrac{27}{4}\right)$.

$y'' = 3x^2 - 6x$.

At $(0,0)$: $f''(0) = 0$, possible point of inflexion.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -0.1 & 0 & 0.1\\ \hline y'' & 0.63 & 0 & -0.57 \end{array}$$

Since concavity changes, $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

At $\left(3,-\dfrac{27}{4}\right)$: $f''(3) = 3(3)^2 - 6(3) = 9 > 0$, a minimum point.

So $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion and $\left(3,-\dfrac{27}{4}\right)$ is a minimum point.

$y'' = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x-2) = 0$, so $x = 0$ ($y = 0$) or $x = 2$ ($y = -4$).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 1.9 & 2 & 2.1\\ \hline y'' & -0.57 & 0 & 0.63 \end{array}$$

Since concavity changes, $(2,-4)$ is a point of inflexion (as is $(0,0)$ from part (a)).

\exfigure{1314_q25_s1}

Endpoints: $x = -1.5$, $y = 4.64$; $x = 4.5$, $y = 11.39$. Minimum at $\left(3,-\dfrac{27}{4}\right)$, horizontal point of inflexion at the origin.

From the right triangle formed by the radius to the midpoint of $AB$: $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{52}{r}$.

$$\dfrac{1 - \log_e x}{x\log_e x} = \dfrac{\frac{1 - \log_e x}{x^2}}{\frac{\log_e x}{x}} = \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx &= \ln\left|\dfrac{\log_e x}{x}\right|_e^{e^2}\\ &= \ln\left[\dfrac{\log_e e^2}{e^2}\right] - \ln\left[\dfrac{\log_e e}{e}\right]\\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{e^2}\right) - \ln\dfrac{1}{e}\\ &= \ln 2 - \ln e^2 + \ln e\\ &= \ln 2 - 2 + 1 = \ln 2 - 1 = \log_e 2 - 1 \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{1314_q30_s1}

Solve simultaneously: $y = 2e^{-x}$ and $y = e^x - 1$.

$$\begin{aligned} e^x - 1 &= \dfrac{2}{e^x}\\ e^{2x} - e^x &= 2\\ (e^x)^2 - e^x - 2 &= 0\\ (e^x - 2)(e^x + 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$e^x = 2$, so $x = \ln 2$ ($e^x = -1$ has no solution). $y = e^{\ln 2} - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1$.

So $P(\ln 2, 1)$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{\ln 2} 2e^{-x} - e^x + 1\,dx\\ &= \left[-2e^{-x} - e^x + x\right]_0^{\ln 2}\\ &= \left[-2e^{-\ln 2} - e^{\ln 2} + \ln 2\right] - \left[-2e^0 - e^0 + 0\right]\\ &= -2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - 2 + \ln 2 + 2 + 1\\ &= \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1314_q32_s1}

Let $m$ be the part of the beam from the ground to the top of the lower wall and $n$ the part from there to the tall wall.

$\sin\alpha = \dfrac{b}{m}$, so $m = \dfrac{b}{\sin\alpha} = b\operatorname{cosec}\alpha$.

$\cos\alpha = \dfrac{a}{n}$, so $n = \dfrac{a}{\cos\alpha} = a\sec\alpha$.

$y = m + n = a\sec\alpha + b\operatorname{cosec}\alpha$

$y = a(\cos\alpha)^{-1} + b(\sin\alpha)^{-1}$

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= -a(\cos\alpha)^{-2}\times(-\sin\alpha) - b(\sin\alpha)^{-2}\times\cos\alpha\\ 0 &= \dfrac{a\sin\alpha}{\cos^2\alpha} - \dfrac{b\cos\alpha}{\sin^2\alpha}\\ 0 &= \dfrac{a\sin^3\alpha - b\cos^3\alpha}{\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\alpha}\\ 0 &= a\sin^3\alpha - b\cos^3\alpha\\ b\cos^3\alpha &= a\sin^3\alpha\\ \dfrac{b}{a} &= \tan^3\alpha\\ \tan\alpha &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{b}{a}} \end{aligned}$$

$\tan^3\alpha = \dfrac{b}{a}$, $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{\sqrt[3]{b}}{\sqrt[3]{a}}$.

$$y' = \dfrac{a\sin\alpha}{\cos^2\alpha} - \dfrac{b\cos\alpha}{\sin^2\alpha}$$

$$y'' = \dfrac{a\cos^3\alpha + 2a\sin^2\alpha\cos\alpha}{\cos^4\alpha} + \dfrac{b\sin^3\alpha + 2b\sin\alpha\cos^2\alpha}{\sin^4\alpha} > 0$$

so this is a minimum point.

$1 + \tan^2\alpha = \sec^2\alpha$, so $1 + \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} = \sec^2\alpha$.

$\cot\alpha = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{a}{b}}$ and $1 + \cot^2\alpha = \operatorname{cosec}^2\alpha$, so $1 + \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} = \operatorname{cosec}^2\alpha$.

$$y = a\sec\alpha + b\operatorname{cosec}\alpha = a\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}} + b\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}$$

\exfigure{1314_q33_s1}
